title: Viral Encephalitis - Counselling a Distressed Parent
patient_instructions: You are Peter, the father of Liam, a 19-year-old man who was brought to hospital by ambulance and is now confused and cannot talk to the doctors himself. You are frightened and want answers. Your story if asked: since yesterday Liam had a headache and felt a bit hot; today he suddenly started behaving strangely and saying things that made no sense, then had a fit (his body shook, he was unresponsive for a minute or two), so you called the ambulance. He has no significant past illness, no drug use that you know of, no recent overseas travel but he was camping in regional Victoria recently. Your IDEAS: you fear he has had a stroke or is 'going mad'. Your CONCERNS: is he going to die, and will he ever be normal again? Your EXPECTATIONS: you want to understand what is wrong and what will be done. Affect: very anxious, tearful, interrupts with worried questions. You calm somewhat if the doctor sits down, is honest, and explains clearly. Ask at least: 'Is it meningitis?', 'Could he have brain damage?', and 'What are you going to do now?'
candidate_instructions: Setting: Emergency department relatives' room. Liam, 19, was admitted confused after a headache, fever and a seizure; he cannot give a history. His CT head is normal and he has no neck stiffness. His father Peter is present and distressed. Tasks: explain the likely diagnosis (delirium due to viral encephalitis) and the investigations, address his concerns, and outline management and implications. You do not need to take a full history or examine the patient. The examiner is looking for a structured, empathetic counselling approach, correct explanation of encephalitis versus meningitis, and a safe management outline.
examiner_instructions: This is primarily a communication/counselling station. The candidate should confirm consent to discuss, use an open question, and explain in plain language that Liam is confused (delirium) due to viral encephalitis - an infection of the brain tissue itself, most commonly herpes simplex, with Japanese encephalitis relevant after regional Victorian camping. Key teaching: encephalitis affects brain FUNCTION (confusion, behaviour change, seizures) whereas meningitis (coverings) gives neck stiffness/photophobia - absent here; a normal CT excludes abscess/tumour. Management the candidate should convey: start IV aciclovir IMMEDIATELY without waiting for CSF PCR; add empirical IV ceftriaxone plus IV dexamethasone if bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded; LP for CSF (lymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose in viral) and CSF viral PCR; note an early HSV PCR can be falsely negative so repeat if suspicion persists; seizure management, notify public health (Japanese encephalitis is notifiable), and urgent transfer to a tertiary centre with neurology/ICU. Reward SPIKES structure, empathy and offering written information/interpreter. Use the rubric.

criteria: Sits down, confirms consent to discuss, uses open question and warning shot
Plain-language explanation, avoids jargon, checks understanding (SPIKES)
Empathy toward distress, invites and answers questions
Offers written information/support (Encephalitis Australia) and interpreter if needed
Explains delirium due to viral encephalitis with reasons (behaviour change, seizure, no neck stiffness, normal CT)
Correctly distinguishes encephalitis from meningitis and gives relevant differentials
Immediate IV aciclovir without waiting for PCR; empirical ceftriaxone + dexamethasone if meningitis not excluded
LP/CSF PCR (with caveat on early false-negative HSV PCR), seizure management, public health notification and tertiary transfer
Explains purpose of CT (excludes structural lesion) and LP/CSF findings
Explains bloods (raised WBC, ESR/CRP) supporting infection

red_flags: Fever, altered mental state and seizure - possible CNS infection requiring immediate empirical treatment
Do not wait for CSF PCR before starting IV aciclovir for suspected HSV encephalitis
Consider bacterial meningitis (non-blanching rash, neck stiffness) - add ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone if it cannot be excluded
Status epilepticus / deteriorating GCS - urgent airway support and ICU/neurology involvement
australian_guidelines: eTG (Encephalitis/Meningitis): start IV aciclovir immediately for suspected HSV encephalitis and do not delay for LP/PCR; add empirical IV ceftriaxone plus IV dexamethasone (with or before the first antibiotic dose) where bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded

Australian public health: Japanese encephalitis virus is a notifiable disease (2022 mainland outbreak - Victoria, NSW, Queensland); notify the local public health unit and send JEV/MVE serology and CSF PCR
eTG seizure management: benzodiazepine first-line then levetiracetam or phenytoin; SPIKES / Medical Board Good Medical Practice for breaking bad news and consent
learning_objectives: Differentiate encephalitis from meningitis clinically and on CSF
Counsel a distressed relative using a structured, empathetic approach
State the immediate empirical treatment of suspected viral encephalitis
Recognise the Australian public-health and transfer implications
key_points: Encephalitis affects brain function (confusion, seizures); meningitis affects the coverings (neck stiffness, photophobia)
Start IV aciclovir immediately - do not wait for PCR; a single early HSV PCR can be falsely negative
A normal CT excludes abscess and tumour; CSF lymphocytosis with normal glucose points to a viral cause
Japanese encephalitis is notifiable and relevant after regional camping in eastern Australia

citations.claim: A febrile patient with altered conscious state and a non-blanching petechial rash is a CNS-infection red flag (meningococcal disease) supporting the meningitis differential.
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment, p.584

citations.claim: Non-viral causes of an encephalitis-like picture include neurosyphilis and other occult bacterial infections requiring a high index of suspicion.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition, p.463

citations.claim: Altered mental state with hallucinations and abnormal behaviour has neurological causes including temporal lobe pathology, relevant to the delirium differential.
citations.source: Churchills Pocketbook of Differential Diagnosis, p.214
